topicA.name: B2B Personalization and the AI-Driven Buyer Journey

resources.headline: AI Raises The Bar For B2B Personalization, Again
resources.fullText: < Featured Blogs Home > Featured Blogs > AI Raises The Bar For B2B Personalization, Again AI Raises The Bar For B2B Personalization, Again Personalized emails, account-specific landing pages, and customized offers can create relevance, but personalization in isolation won’t meet the needs of empowered, AI-assisted B2B buyers. B2B buyers and customers expect providers to understand their goals, recognize their context, and deliver relevant experiences throughout the buying journey and postsale experience. Companies that cannot deliver on those expectations risk forfeiting conversion, acquisition, and expansion opportunities while losing relevance and influence in increasingly digital and AI-mediated buying journeys. B2B marketers face mounting pressure to deliver relevant, valuable content and digital experiences that influence both human and AI audiences. Yet despite widespread utilization, many B2B companies struggle to mature personalization beyond isolated tactics. Instead, they create experiences that feel generic, disconnected, or focused on the seller rather than the buyer. Personalizing An Asset Or Delivery Mechanism Isn’t Enough As buyers move from exploring a problem to building consensus and justifying a decision, their information needs change. Personalized experiences must adapt accordingly in the moment of need. B2B personalization should respond to the buyer’s context and information questions, reducing complexity early in the journey. As purchase decisions progress, personalization must continue to support consensus, business justification, and commitment. This requires a combination of personalization techniques, decisioning, and orchestration capabilities that are audience led, channel independent, and AI enabled. B2B marketers most commonly use segment-based targeting, personalize for personas, and personalize based on behavior. Personalization based on buyer need is most impactful but not among the topmost utilized techniques. Effective B2B personalization approaches combine audience-centric design, buying group awareness, signal activation, connected content, and composable experiences. The resulting interaction experiences are contextual, conditional, and increasingly conversational to help increase relevance, influence decisions, and drive customer value. Use AI To Close The Gap Between Content Generation And Real-Time Personalization Forrester’s Marketing Survey, 2026 found that 88% of B2B marketing leaders say personalization is an AI use case in full production, pilot, proof of concept, or experimentation phase. Content creation continues to be a leading AI use case for B2B personalization. In Forrester’s B2B Marketing Online Community B2B Summit Survey, March 2026, 71% of respondents said they use AI to generate or adapt content variations for different audiences or contexts. Yet only 23% use AI to assemble or adapt experiences in real time based on interaction context, intent, and signals. The broader opportunity to capture value from AI spanning B2B personalization workflows includes: Delivering contextual relevance in the moment of interaction. Capturing new signals from the content that audiences consume and the actions they take. Using those signals to inform more meaningful personalization of the next interaction. Putting B2B Personalization In Context AI can expand and accelerate capabilities in each of the B2B personalization competency areas of strategy, data, design, delivery, and measurement. It’s a path toward moving beyond static segmentation, planned content sequences, and delivery mechanism silos. The result? Dynamically personalized, buying-group-aware experiences that reflect real-time buyer behaviors. Agentic AI expands the B2B personalization playbook through shared context, memory, autonomy, and collaboration across digital marketing workflows. This changes how work gets done and how buyers engage. Agentic AI also enables new personalization channels and modalities like conversational websites and avatars, effectively combining individualized knowledge with its delivery mechanism. For all the new capabilities and innovation opportunities AI brings to B2B personalization, its fundamental goal remains unchanged: to deliver the most relevant information and experience in the moment of interaction based on who the audience is, where they are in their journey, and what they’re trying to accomplish. Check out the new report, Forrester’s Essential Guide To B2B Personalization, on the core concepts, frameworks, and practical guidance that marketing leaders need to build, scale, mature, and measure B2B personalization, and chat with Forrester AI to learn what it means for your business and your buyers (Forrester clients only). Related Forrester Content Forrester’s Essential Guide To B2B Personalization Personalization Should Pervade The Entire Customer Lifecycle, Not Just The Buying Journey The Forrester B2B Personalization Deployment Model Categories Account-Based Marketing (ABM) AI Insights B2B Marketing personalization
keyNotes: Even if you send personalized emails or special landing pages, that's often not enough because today's business buyers (who are also using AI to help them) expect companies to truly understand their specific goals and situation throughout their entire buying process.

While a large majority (71%) of B2B marketers are using AI to create or adjust content for different audiences, far fewer (only 23%) are using AI to actually build or change entire customer experiences in real-time based on what a buyer is doing right now.

Surprisingly, the most effective way to personalize for business customers is by understanding their specific needs at that moment, but this powerful technique isn't among the most commonly used by marketers.
AI is changing how companies personalize by allowing them to move beyond simple, pre-planned messages to create dynamic, real-time experiences that adapt instantly to what a group of buyers is doing.
resources.question: The article points out that while many use AI to create content, far fewer use it to adapt entire experiences in real-time based on what someone is doing or needing right now. In your own field, where could you move beyond just creating static information and instead use technology to dynamically adjust your approach to better meet someone's immediate, evolving needs?

resources.headline: Why Building Trust Through Real People Stands The Test Of Time In SEO & AI Search via @sejournal, @lilyraynyc
resources.fullText: When it comes to organic search marketing, a loophole is not a strategy. Loopholes have expiration dates, and in many cases, the time spent chasing them would have been better spent on work that doesn’t backfire later on. Any SEO who has worked in the field for a while has inevitably lived through a seemingly endless loop of fads, hype cycles, and shortcuts aimed at tricking search engines (and now, AI systems). Exact-match domains, article directories, parasite SEO, guest posting at scale, PBNs, programmatic pages, and now the AI-generated listicles, scaled AI content, and “inauthentic mentions” of the GEO era. Most of these things work for a while… until they don’t. And once Google, Bing, and more recently the AI companies themselves crack down, the sites that leaned on these approaches often end up worse off than if they’d never tried them at all, sometimes spending years cleaning up while traffic, visibility, and leads stay suppressed. Plenty of people in this industry have battle scars from these experiences, myself included. My first real SEO wins came from buying links in 2010-2011, and Penguin erased them in a single morning in 2012. Six years later, the 2018 “Medic” update hit a client of ours that had been using AI and automation to scale medical content (long before this was popular), and it was the hardest hit from an algorithm update that I had experienced firsthand since the Penguin update. I think these scars are the badge of honor that inevitably comes with experience in SEO: thinking you know better than Google, and learning the hard way that you almost always don’t. All of that said, there is one investment that has held up through every one of those cycles, and it’s the same approach I’ve recommended for many years: investing in real humans and placing them at the center of your marketing strategy. As AI makes generic content nearly free to produce, I believe that real, identifiable experts are becoming the clearest antidote to scaled, machine-generated slop. This article covers why, what the evidence shows so far, and how brands can consider “human-centric marketing” as a bigger part of their strategies. Google Has Been Saying The Same Thing For 20+ Years What I find interesting, looking back, is how consistent Google’s guidance has been the entire time, if you read between the lines (or read the guidelines at all). Google’s Webmaster Guidelines from 2003 (yes, 23 years ago) already told site owners to “make pages for users, not for search engines,” and warned against “cookie cutter” approaches with “little or no original content.” They even said that site owners following the spirit of the guidelines would do better than “those who spend their time looking for loopholes they can exploit.” Google’s Webmaster Guidelines as of December 2003, via the Wayback Machine. (Image Credit: Lily Ray) The list of spam violations Google laid out back then has carried on, in some form, for more than 20 years, right into the AI search era. I put together this infographic showing how Google’s original spam policies map to popular GEO tactics we see today with AI search: Google’s 2003 quality guidelines, side by side with popular AI search tactics in 2026. (Image Credit: Lily Ray) Automation in particular has been in the crosshairs for well over a decade. In August 2010, Google’s John Mueller told a site owner that publishing Google Translate output directly “could be seen as creating auto-generated content, which would be against our Webmaster Guidelines,” and recommended having a human correct it first. By 2012, Google had published a dedicated help page on automatically generated content. Its examples included text “translated by an automated tool without human review or curation,” Markov chains, automated synonymizing, scraped feeds, and “stitching or combining content from different web pages without adding sufficient value.” Google’s help page on automatically generated content, October 2012, via the Wayback Machine. (Image Credit: Lily Ray) For what it’s worth, I still see this exact issue affecting sites today – perhaps more than ever – including companies who come to me after experimenting with scaled AI translations that get little human review. It’s interesting that John’s 15+ year old answer still holds up, although to be fair, most site owners have never read Google’s guidelines (and nobody can be expected to know about a forum reply from 2010). That’s what their SEO experts are (supposedly) there to help them with. Funny enough, that 2012 list reads a lot like the sales pitch for the same AI content tools that have recently captured the attention of C-level marketers everywhere, many of which work in ways that come very close to (if not directly violate) Google’s long-standing anti-spam policies. It’s not a huge surprise that so many of the sites featured in their case studies have since rapidly lost organic traffic. Google’s wording has evolved since then, but the thread running through it has stayed remarkably consistent. In February 2023, a few months after ChatGPT launched, Google said it has “many years of experience dealing with automation being used in an attempt to game search results.” Then in March 2024, Google launched the scaled content abuse spam policy, which applies whether content is made “through automation, human efforts, or some combination of human and automated processes.” Automated translation, synonymizing, and stitching are still on the list, 14 years later. Marketers are now using LLMs to experiment heavily with all three. The main difference now is that generative AI sits at the top of the list of examples. Across more than 20 years of guidelines, the common thread is fairly simple: content made for search engines at scale, with no human reviewing it, adding to it, or standing behind it, eventually becomes a liability. E-E-A-T Gave Us A Way Out Of The Loop When Google started using the acronym “E-A-T” in 2014 (now called “E-E-A-T”), it finally ga
keyNotes: Trying to find quick ways to trick search engines (like Google) often backfires, causing websites to lose traffic and visibility later on. The author personally experienced this when a shortcut they used in 2010-2011 was penalized by Google in 2012.

For over 20 years, Google has consistently advised website owners to create content for real people, not just for search engines, warning against "cookie cutter" or automated content. They even said this in their guidelines from 2003.

Even though new AI tools can create content cheaply, Google has warned against using automated content without human review since at least 2010, and this warning still applies today. Many sites using these new AI tools have seen their traffic drop.

The most reliable way to succeed in online marketing, especially with so much machine-made content, is to focus on real people and their expertise in your strategy. This means having identifiable experts create and stand behind your content.
resources.question: The article highlights that trying to find quick ways to trick search engines often backfires, while focusing on real people and their expertise consistently works over time. In your own work, where might you be tempted to take a shortcut or automate a process, and what would it look like to instead invest in a more human-centered approach for long-term success?

resources.headline: The Art, Science and Theater of Modern Marketing ft. Thomas Ranese
resources.fullText: By Jenny Rooney What if the best marketing advantage you have is something that cannot be replicated by an algorithm?For Thomas Ranese, CMO of Intuit, it starts with theater, empathy and understanding what people are actually trying to achieve.In this episode of Marketing Vanguard, Jenny Rooney sits down with Thomas to unpack how an unconventional career spanning theater, Google and Uber shaped his approach to marketing leadership. From growing up behind the counter of his father’s pasta shop to leading marketing at one of the world’s biggest financial technology platforms, Thomas gets into why emotional connection can be just as powerful as performance data.He also addresses why AI needs human expertise to earn customer trust, and why brands should bring more humanity, creativity, and purpose into modern marketing.What you’ll learn: How Thomas’s background in theater, consulting and government became an unexpected advantage in marketing Why marketing is a form of theater that extends beyond advertising into customer experience and retail Why empathy and emotional connection can make marketers more effective in a performance-driven world Why AI and human expertise need to work together, particularly in high-stakes financial services Why brands should position their products as enablers of customer ambitions rather than the end goal How Intuit connects its mission of powering prosperity with financial literacy and business growth Why CMOs need to stay hands-on with technology, creative execution and customer experience as organizations scale How to make bold marketing work through humor, creativity and a better understanding of what customers need About the guest: Thomas Ranese is Chief Marketing Officer at Intuit, a global technology platform serving millions of customers worldwide with TurboTax, QuickBooks, Credit Karma and Mailchimp. His career has taken him through some very different worlds, including theater, consulting, government and nonprofit work, Google and Uber. His approach to marketing is rooted in a simple idea: understand what people are trying to achieve, then build brands and experiences that help them get there. He strongly believes in storytelling and using humor to make complex information more relatable. At Intuit, Thomas is helping shape the company’s evolution into an integrated, AI-powered financial technology platform, with a focus on combining technology with human expertise to help consumers and businesses prosper.Episode Highlights: 07:18 Marketing Is Theater, and It Goes Beyond Advertising — Thomas breaks down the three different kinds of theater that shape modern marketing: the storytelling and drama of advertising, the emotions and interactions built into customer experience, and the immersive experiences brands create through retail. He also believes real-world human interactions will become increasingly important as more of our lives move into digital and AI-powered environments. 12:44 What a Pasta Shop Taught Him About Customer Obsession — Thomas traces his interest in marketing back to his childhood, when he spent time working in his father’s small pasta shop. He loved being behind the counter, helping customers and figuring out what they needed. He even created his father’s first promotional newsletter on a Commodore 64. Looking back, he sees those early experiences as the foundation of his approach to customer connection, communication and service.16:01 Why AI Needs Human Intelligence Too — Intuit is building AI into the core of its financial technology platform, but Thomas is particularly focused on the role human experts play alongside it. When customers are making important decisions about taxes, credit or their businesses, getting the right answer matters. AI can provide powerful technology and efficiency, but human expertise brings verification, empathy and the confidence customers need to act.19:57 Money Is a Means to an End. So Is Your Product — Thomas challenges brands to think beyond what their products do and focus on what customers want to achieve with them. Small business owners aren’t necessarily starting businesses because they want to make money; they’re pursuing a craft, building a lifestyle, serving customers or creating opportunities for their families. The same principle applies across categories: brands become more meaningful when they understand the bigger ambitions their products help people achieve.22:00 Intuit’s Goal for Financial Literacy — Thomas explains how Intuit is connecting its mission to power prosperity with financial literacy education. Through Intuit for Education, the company aims to reach 50 million students by 2030, addressing the fact that only 32% of students graduate able to pass a basic financial literacy exam. For Thomas, this is an opportunity to create meaningful social impact while building trust and introducing a new generation to the tools that can help them succeed.26:02 Why CMOs Should be Fully Involved — Thomas pushes back on the idea that senior marketing leaders should step away from execution as their organizations grow. With technology and AI changing marketing so quickly, he believes CMOs need to stay hands-on, understand the tools and continue learning. He argues that the bigger the organization, the more important this becomes, especially when it is easy to become disconnected from the actual work and the customers being served. Jenny Rooney Jenny Rooney is Chief Brand and Community Officer, leading strategy for the overall ADWEEK brand as well as the ways in which we serve and support our audiences with high-value content, products, partnerships and experiences, notably through our community programs such as Marketing Vanguard. @jenny_rooney| jenny.rooney@adweek.com
keyNotes: Surprisingly, marketing isn't just about ads; it's like a play with three acts: the storytelling in advertising, the emotions customers feel during their experience, and the immersive environments brands create in places like stores.

Even with powerful Artificial Intelligence (AI) making things efficient, human experts are still essential for building trust, providing empathy, and giving customers the confidence they need, especially for important decisions like managing finances.

Instead of just selling what a product does, the best marketing focuses on what customers *really* want to achieve with it, like how a small business owner might use a tool to pursue a passion or build a family legacy, not just to make money.

Even as companies grow, top marketing leaders (like a Chief Marketing Officer or CMO) need to stay actively involved with new technology, creative ideas, and understanding customer experiences, so they don't get disconnected from the real work.
resources.question: The article highlights that products are just tools to help people achieve bigger goals, like how a small business owner might use software to pursue a passion, not just make money. Thinking about your own work, what deeper ambition or dream are you helping your customers or colleagues achieve, beyond the immediate task or transaction?

resources.headline: Salesforce CEO Says ‘Goodbye SEO.’ Salesforce’s SEO Guide Disagrees via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern
resources.fullText: On Nov. 18, Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff said “Goodbye SEO” on X, promoting Palmata, an AI-based tool for tracking how visible a company is in AI answers, while a Salesforce guide linked on Palmata’s page states SEO “is still the foundation.” Benioff wrote in his post that customers “aren’t searching anymore” but instead are asking Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini and other AI assistants which brands they should purchase. The post further states, “No click. No referral. Nothing in your analytics,” and then pitches Palmata as a tool that monitors what AI assistants say about a business, offers recommendations on what changes need to be made, and simulates the effect of those changes prior to publication. Several SEO professionals countered Benioff’s claims in quote posts and replies. What Salesforce’s Pages Say Salesforce’s guide to SEO and AEO (answer engine optimization) says SEO “isn’t going away” and that “SEO is still the foundation.” Graham Hardt, whose byline lists him as SEO Senior Director, wrote it for new businesses, and Salesforce published it Sept. 11. Palmata’s product page links to the guide from its FAQ. Screenshot from the Salesforce SEO and AEO guide. Highlight added. Contentful introduced Palmata in June; it became a part of Salesforce when Salesforce’s acquisition of Contentful occurred on Sept. 1. The article announcing the launch of Palmata, written by Jason McGhee, head of product and engineering for Palmata, said that SEO gave organizations “a practical framework for improving visibility” and added, “That work remains essential.” How SEO Professionals Responded Aleyda Solis, an SEO and AI search consultant who founded Orainti, wrote in a quote post that AI search “relies on many of the same fundamentals as SEO.” Her post continues, “AI search optimization goes beyond traditional SEO, but it certainly doesn’t replace it.” Solis also wrote that measuring AI search visibility matters, “but monitoring what AI platforms say about your brand and actually improving your visibility, recommendations and business outcomes are very different things.” Pedro Dias, a technical SEO product manager who used to work at Google, wrote that SEO “was never a topic that attracted the interest of decision makers.” His post adds, “SEO isn’t traffic. It never has been.” Lily Ray, who founded Algorythmic, replied to Benioff, “This gold rush already happened and the market is already oversaturated.” Growth advisor Eli Schwartz wrote that “there’s yet another AEO tool in the mix.” Why This Matters When Benioff’s post is read by a marketing executive, Salesforce’s own guide answers it, stating that SEO and AEO are “two visibility layers for the same audience.” In terms of making the case for new businesses to include both SEO and AEO, this guide provides Salesforce’s reasoning for including SEO in your plans right alongside any AI visibility tool, such as Palmata. Looking Ahead According to Palmata’s FAQ section, Palmata is a standalone tool that is also built into Marketing Cloud by Salesforce. In weighing tools like Palmata, Salesforce’s guide says you should track “both sets of metrics.” This means tracking your organic traffic and rankings, but also tracking how many times you’ve been cited by AI. Featured Image: Thrive Studios ID/Shutterstock Category News SEO
keyNotes: The head of a major tech company, Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff, recently declared that making your website easy for people to find through search engines (which marketers call SEO) is obsolete because customers are now asking AI assistants like ChatGPT for recommendations instead.

Surprisingly, a guide published by Salesforce itself, written by their SEO Senior Director, says the exact opposite, stating that making your website easy to find (SEO) "is still the foundation" for businesses.

The CEO believes that when people get answers from AI, there's "No click. No referral. Nothing in your analytics," meaning companies won't be able to track how customers found them through traditional methods.

To address this new way customers find information, Salesforce is promoting a tool called Palmata, which helps companies monitor what AI assistants say about them and suggests ways to improve their visibility in AI answers.

Despite the CEO's strong statement, Salesforce's own guide advises businesses to track both traditional website traffic (how many people visit their site) and how often AI assistants mention them, suggesting both are important.
resources.question: The article shows a big company's CEO saying one way customers find products (like through search engines) is "goodbye," while his own company's experts say it's "still the foundation." In your own work, how do you decide when to completely abandon an old, established method for a new technology, especially when there's conflicting advice?

resources.question: The article highlights that creating a lot of content just for search engines, without real people reviewing or standing behind it, eventually causes problems. In your own work or industry, where might the temptation to prioritize speed or quantity over genuine human expertise lead to long-term issues, and how could you ensure human quality remains central?

keyNotes: One company, BirdEye, spent $6.4 million on search engine ads and managed to cut the cost of getting a potential customer interested by 43%. They achieved this by improving how their ads were shown and understanding which ads actually led to customers.

Another company, Qualys, spent $9.6 million and improved how many potential customers became real sales opportunities by 31%. They achieved this by carefully tracking how customers interacted with them to find out where their spending wasn't working.

A marketing agency found that combining all their online advertising efforts into one plan, instead of treating them separately, grew their potential deals by 25% and got 50% more interested visitors. This shows that a unified strategy can be more effective than separate ones.

For a company called Arm, they shortened the time it took to close a sale by 18% by focusing their marketing efforts on specific, important companies. This targeted approach helped them move deals faster.

A consumer technology brand, iBaby Labs, got 34% more website visitors and 20% more people taking desired actions without spending extra money. They did this by simply improving how they handled potential customer inquiries.
